title: Passover: clearing out
hook: the house is cleared of leaven; teachers call it clearing out puffed-up pride
tomorrow: Passover: a candle and a feather

segments.voice: Yesterday, the masks of Purim, and a book where God is hidden. Your line was who's under the mask. Did you ask someone how they really are? Purim is a month before Passover, and the cleaning starts now. Day six hundred seventy-six.

In the weeks before Passover, observant Jewish homes go a little wild. Couch cushions come off. Car seats get vacuumed for cereal. Coat pockets are turned inside out for old cookies. The toaster gets put away, or given away. Kitchen cabinets are emptied and taped shut. Someone finds a pretzel behind the fridge from two Passovers ago. It looks like spring cleaning, and in a way it is. But the target is very specific. People aren't hunting for dust. They're hunting for one thing, and the Torah gives it a name.
screen: `CUSHIONS OFF, POCKETS OUT.` → `A PRETZEL BEHIND THE FRIDGE.` → `HUNTING FOR ONE THING.`

segments.voice: The word is chametz: leaven, or anything that has risen. In Jewish law, chametz is grain from five kinds, wheat, barley, spelt, rye and oats, that has mixed with water and been left long enough to ferment. Bread, pasta, cake, beer, cereal. The Torah is firm about it. In the old Jewish translation: "seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; howbeit the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses." And not just don't eat it. Don't own it. Don't let it be seen in your home. That's why the cleaning goes into the pockets and the car. Why leaven? The plain answer is the story itself. Leaving Egypt, the Israelites had no time to let their dough rise, so they baked it flat. Matzah is the bread of hurry. But the rabbis heard something more in it. In the Talmud, tractate Berakhot, a rabbi named Alexandri prays that God knows what really stops us from doing God's will: the yeast in the dough. The rabbis used that image for the inner pull toward wrong. Later, Hasidic teachers made it personal. Chametz puffs up. It takes a little substance and fills it with air until it looks bigger than it is. That, they said, is pride. Matzah is just flour and water, flat, nothing added. Another teaching points out that in Hebrew, chametz and matzah are spelled with almost the same letters. The difference between them is one small stroke. So the cleaning of the house becomes a cleaning of the self: looking into the corners for anything that's swollen past its size.
screen: `CHAMETZ: GRAIN THAT HAS RISEN.` · `PUT AWAY LEAVEN FROM YOUR HOUSES.` · `THE YEAST IN THE DOUGH.` · `PUFFED UP, OR FLAT.` · then, large: `CLEAR OUT THE PUFFED-UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear one crumb-filled corner. If you can, go now to one small spot, a drawer, a bag, a car cup holder, and clear it out while you breathe. If you can't move, picture it. Then, as the bell holds, look inward the same way. Is there one place you've been puffed up lately: a story you've inflated, an opinion you've held too loudly, a credit you took that wasn't all yours? Just notice it. Let it shrink back to its real size. The bell holds the time.
Chametz. Leaven, grain that has risen: cleared out of the house before Passover, and for many teachers, a picture of pride. Today's word.
Your line: clear out the puffed-up. Today, when you catch yourself making something sound bigger than it is, say it again, smaller and true. Day six hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: In the weeks before Passover, observant Jews clean their homes, cars and workplaces of chametz, use separate Passover dishes, and formally sell or renounce any chametz they still own before the festival begins.

fork.setup: the Israelites are leaving Egypt tonight. the bread dough is mixed, but it hasn't risen. what do they do?
options: wait for the dough to rise.
bake it flat and take it with them.
fork.reveal: they baked it as it was, unleavened: there wasn't time. matzah is the bread of hurry.

original.note: Hebrew: leaven, anything that has risen and fermented.

trapdoor: what you thought: Passover cleaning is spring cleaning.
what it means: the target is chametz, leaven, which may not be owned or seen during the festival.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 12:15 and 13:7, Mishnah Pesachim's five grains, Berakhot 17a's yeast in the dough as the inner pull, and the Hasidic reading of chametz as pride.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): narrowed "Jewish homes" to observant homes, replaced stock "teachers have long heard", dropped "well-known".
Exodus 12:15 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify ('Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; howbeit the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses').
Mishnah Pesachim 2:5 lists the five grains for matzah (and thus chametz); verify reference.
Berakhot 17a: Rabbi Alexandri's prayer naming 'the yeast in the dough' and 'subjugation to the kingdoms'; paraphrased.
Hasidic chametz-as-pride teaching attributed generally; the chet/heh spelling observation is a popular homily, labeled as 'a well-known teaching'.
Customs (selling chametz, separate dishes) vary by community.
